#1046. Uefa announces candidate to challenge Gianni Infantino for Fifa presidency

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Gianni Infantino is seeking a fourth term as Fifa president despite criticism from governing bodies including Uefa

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Gianni Infantino will face a challenge from French Football Federation president Philippe Diallo in next year's Fifa presidential election.

National association representatives on Uefa's executive committee have invited Diallo to stand and given him their unanimous backing.

Uefa said Diallo will stand and this was formally ratified following an executive committee meeting at the French Football Federation’s headquarters in Paris on Tuesday. The move follows Arsene Wenger ruling himself out of a challenge to Infantino over the weekend.

Uefa pledged in August to identify a credible alternative candidate to Infantino. That pledge came after the body said it had lost confidence in the Swiss over his plan to seek private investment in a company to run the commercial aspects of the World Cup and other Fifa competitions.

A Uefa statement said: "Against the backdrop of serious concerns over the direction of Fifa, the national associations called for renewed unity and trust within the global football community.

“They also called for a Fifa that places the development of the game in every region of the world at the heart of its mission, upholds the highest standards of governance and works in close partnership with its member associations, confederations and football stakeholders. They expressed their full confidence in Philippe Diallo to provide the leadership needed to achieve this ambition.”

Diallo, who said he wasn’t initially intending to enter the presidential race, says he wants to restore what is now “broken” trust in football’s governance after Infantino seemed to act alone in his privatisation plans, while the creation of a peace prize for US president Donald Trump and the Folarin Balogun red card debacle also sparked huge concerns.

“It created a situation this summer whereby the trust placed in Fifa and it’s president was broken," Diallo said. “They have damaged the image of football and have introduced the poison of division.”

Diallo faces a tough challenge to unseat Infantino, who will be standing for a fourth term as Fifa president.

Infantino appeared to be on the ropes in August when his private investor plan was rejected by three continents and a number of key allies expressing their concern at how it had been developed.

He has since rallied support, however, and is expected to receive strong backing in Africa, Asia, Oceania and South America.

Japanese FA honorary president Kozo Tashima had earlier declared his intention to stand, as has former Tottenham defender Ramon Vega.

Germany head coach Jurgen Klopp has called for a change of leadership in Fifa, claiming Infantino compares unfavourably to his predecessor Sepp Blatter, who resigned in 2015 amid allegations of corruption.

In quotes reported by the BBC, Klopp said: "I've been following football for many years. There are people who are much more knowledgeable about this than I am. But I think most people now agree a change would make a lot of sense.

“I didn’t think things could get worse after Sepp Blatter, but someone has managed to do just that.”

Klopp added: “Regarding Gianni Infantino, surely the next person to come along can do a better job.”

Liftoff is scheduled for 5:45 p.m. ET today (Nov. 13).

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap.

SpaceX plans to launch its Starship megarocket on an unprecedented mission today (Nov. 13), and you can watch the action live.

Starship is scheduled to launch on its 15th test flight today from SpaceX's Starbase site in South Texas, during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). SpaceX plans to bring both of Starship's stages back to Starbase for a catch by the launch tower's "chopstick" arms — something it has never done before.

You can watch it all live here at Space.com. And there should be a lot to see: Starship Flight 15 will last more than 22 hours, if all goes according to plan.

Starship consists of two elements: a huge booster known as Super Heavy and an upper-stage spacecraft called Starship, or Ship for short. Both are designed to be fully and rapidly reusable — a first in the world of orbital spaceflight.

The rapidity of Starship's reuse hinges heavily on SpaceX's recovery strategy: Returning both vehicles directly to the launch mount will enable much faster inspection, refurbishment and reflight, the company has said.

SpaceX has already caught Super Heavy, pulling the feat off on three previous Starship test flights. But it has never tried to do so with Ship, which flies farther and faster than the booster and is therefore a more challenging vehicle to recover.

So today's flight is a pretty big deal for SpaceX.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," the company wrote in a Flight 15 mission description.

The action will unspool over two days, if all goes to plan. Super Heavy will return to Starbase for a touchdown just 6.5 minutes after launch, but Ship will continue on to low Earth orbit.

The upper stage will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites, during a 42-minute stretch beginning about 35 minutes after liftoff. This will be just the second batch of V3 spacecraft to reach orbit, after the 26 that went up on Flight 14 on Sept. 28.

Ship will then stay aloft for nearly a full day. The mission plan calls for the upper stage to return to Starbase for its chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), about 22.5 hours after liftoff.

There's no guarantee things will go according to plan, however. SpaceX will call off a Ship catch if the vehicle experiences any issues during Flight 15. If something crops up, the company will steer Ship to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, either near Hawaii or off the coast of Chile.

So it'll be a busy weekend for SpaceX, and for space fans who want to keep tabs on the mission. And we can help you out there, with our Flight 15 updates page.

#1044. Who is standing for Fifa president – and can anyone finally topple Gianni Infantino?

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Gianni Infantino appears in pole position to win the election, but may not have things all his own way this time

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Gianni Infantino remains in a strong position to secure a further four-year mandate as Fifa president, even after enduring significant pushback over his governance.

However, a number of challengers have stepped forward ahead of next March’s election. So, who is in the running to potentially oust Infantino, and do they realistically have a chance of beating him?

To be eligible, candidates require backing from at least five member associations and must demonstrate active involvement as a player or official within Fifa, a confederation or a national association for two of the preceding five years.

Every one of Fifa's 211 member associations holds a single vote, meaning national size or historical success carries no extra weight. Consequently, world champions Spain possess identical voting power to San Marino, who sit bottom of the world rankings.

When two or fewer contenders stand, victory requires a simple majority - exceeding 50 per cent - of the valid votes submitted.

In races with three or more candidates, a two-thirds majority of present and eligible member associations is needed in the initial round. Should subsequent ballots be required, the candidate receiving the fewest votes is knocked out in each round until two remain.

Formal nominations close on Wednesday, four months prior to the assembly. Voting will subsequently occur during the 77th Fifa Congress in Rabat on 18 March.

The Fifa general secretariat is required to inform member associations of the official candidates for president no later than one month before the Congress convenes.

Discontent mounted following proposals for the Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE), an initiative designed to introduce private funding into a fresh entity overseeing commercial rights for premier Fifa tournaments, such as the World Cup.

Opponents targeted both the structural details of the initiative and the absence of consultation and openness with which it was introduced to Fifa's membership.

The backlash grew so severe that prominent administrators urged Infantino to step down, while multiple regional confederations formed a united front, prompting the president to eventually scrap the plan.

Having withdrawn the FFE plan following threats from European body Uefa to boycott Fifa fixtures, Infantino offered an apology to the Fifa Council regarding the management of the proposal.

While Uefa - among three confederations that had demanded his resignation - remained unmoved, the apology served to mend bridges with the Asian Football Confederation (AFC).

AFC head Sheikh Salman bin Ibrahim Al Khalifa, who had denounced the project as a "fundamental breach of trust", subsequently changed position to offer his endorsement to the president.

Elsewhere, South American governing body Conmebol declined to demand Infantino's departure, while the Confederation of African Football (CAF) maintained solid backing.

A pledge by Infantino to distribute $25m to every member association also seems to have been instrumental in smoothing over tensions.

Concacaf, representing North America, Central America and the Caribbean, originally aligned with Uefa and the AFC in voicing opposition. However, its delegation has since split, with Mexico alongside various Caribbean nations rallying behind Infantino.

As one of the most seasoned figures in the race, Tashima has outlined ambitions to reform Fifa's governance, rebuild institutional accountability and tackle what he views as an unhealthy centralisation of authority.

Possessing deep internal knowledge of the governing body's inner workings, the Japanese administrator offers a direct proposition: "I'll keep what's good and change what's bad."

Diallo entered the contest relatively late, gathering support from Uefa member associations sitting on both its executive committee and the Fifa Council.

In charge of the FFF since 2023, the Frenchman has consistently challenged Infantino's leadership. Nonetheless, Uefa has stopped short of confirming unanimous backing from its 55 member nations, leaving his exact level of support uncertain.

Vega grounds his platform in athletic credentials, commercial background and ten years of global campaigning, with the former defender stating he has travelled to over 140 nations to build support.

His bid is far from impulsive given his prior campaigns for office, yet three prior failures create doubts over whether his ambitions can translate into meaningful voting power.

#1043. Man Utd are in relegation trouble and Carrick must be sacked

Michael Carrick stood perfectly still and raised his left arm, and his index finger, high in the air. Around him, chaos. As it had been all afternoon. Substitute Patrick Dorgu had just headed in a corner to rescue a point for Manchester United in the 96th minute and, maybe, save Carrick his job.

Going into added time and United were two goals behind. It seemed all was lost for them against Aston Villa and for their head coach, but how telling was the reaction, in the directors’ box, of chief executive Omar Berrada and director of football Jason Wilcox, who both jumped up in celebration? They were far more animated than Carrick and could not contain themselves.

"Football is a contact sport!" 🗣️ Did Senne Lammens foul Zion Suzuki for Man United's equaliser? 🤔 https://t.co/KCb1lHqPHP

Did their behaviour betray not just their excitement in the moment but their relief at not having to sack Carrick during this forthcoming international break? If so, they need to think again. They need to make a sober and rational decision based on evidence. And the evidence shows that Carrick must go. Because this kind of football is unsustainable. This kind of football does not work. This kind of football is stupid.

United are 18th in the Premier League. They have won one game in 10 in the league. They have conceded 15 goals in their last five matches in the league and Champions League. When they play Liverpool away, their next game, on November 22, it will be the first time they have done so from inside the relegation zone since March 1937.

They appear shockingly disorganised. Tactics seem to be an after-thought, their motivation is lacking until desperation kicks in. United conceded two goals within four minutes at the start of the game. And then two more within eight minutes of the second half kicking off.

The bottom line is this: can they afford not to make a change? If they do not, United could be accused of copping out and gambling with their status. So, Berrada and Wilcox must ask: what is Carrick doing in the dressing room and on the training ground? What messages are he and his assistant Steve Holland sending out? Are the players even listening?

At the end the fans sang Carrick’s name after United became the first team in the Premier League to come back twice from being two goals down. That also summed up the fog of confusion at a club who so obviously lack direction – from the top down – and need to get a grip of themselves. Carrick talked about having to “tighten up” the defending. But everything needs to be stronger. More taut. More competitive.

Chaos can be entertaining. Chaos can be fun. As an advert for the Premier League this was outstanding. United fans will be thrilled with the Fergie-time comeback. But chaos is also unsustainable. No one knows what to expect from United.

In the cold light of day Villa manager Unai Emery will have to ask himself whether he, too, got it wrong. His substitutions did not work, bizarrely taking off too much experience, such as his outstanding captain John McGinn, and he handed United a late initiative when it looked like all hope was lost.

But analyse the goals that United conceded. Any rational response would suggest a change should be made. Take the first two. Villa scored with their first attack, moving the ball from a throw-in, with zero pressure on them, from left to right with McGinn finding Alysson. The winger’s low first-time shot went through the legs of goalkeeper Senne Lammens, who had an awful game. Lammens’s only positive contribution was to come up for the late corner from which Dorgu scored, possibly getting away with a sly nudge on Villa’s Zion Suzuki.

What a start for Aston Villa! 🔥 Alysson fires home to give the the visitors the lead https://t.co/F0nfSRMWRa

Then Lammens conceded a second as he fumbled a shot from Alysson, after the Brazilian was again teed up by McGinn with Nicolas Jackson tucking home the rebound. It followed a poor defensive header from Leny Yoro. It would not be his last one.

Nicolas Jackson has made it 2-0 to Aston Villa after just 4 minutes and boos ring out around Old Trafford 🤯 https://t.co/G7oWDNMjGS

At that point, even so early, it felt over. For United. For Carrick. Then it got complicated. In fairness, United responded brilliantly. By half-time it was 2-2 and a potentially mutinous situation, with the fans on edge and unfurling new banners attacking the hierarchy – including one which read “your funeral not ours” – had turned and were raucous in a positive way.

Matheus Cunha, with a sharp turn and run into the Villa penalty area before being brought down, earned the spot kick from which Bruno Fernandes pulled back the first goal. Former Villa midfielder Youri Tielemans drew them level with a first-time shot. Not just that but they peppered the Villa goal.

Youri Tielemans against his former club! 😱 Manchester United are level just before the break! https://t.co/8kFOQkl814

Then they conceded two more in quick succession with a ridiculous trip on Alysson by Diogo Dalot, who was given the runaround at left-back until he was substituted to cheers. McGinn scored from the penalty. It was 4-2 when Yoro inexplicably headed a McGinn free-kick goalwards, Lammens tipped it on to the crossbar and Leon Goretzka eventually bundled the ball in.

Tellingly, the United supporters appeared too stunned to protest. The game meandered to what felt like an inevitable conclusion, petering out much like, surely, Carrick’s time in charge.

But, football, bloody hell. As someone – who was appointed United manager 40 years ago last week – once said. Dorgu made a difference. As did Joshua Zirkzee, another substitute, as the pair became United’s unlikely saviours, the striker sweeping home the full-back’s cross in the 92nd minute, with six added on.

Then a corner was won. The roar went up – as did Lammens. But it was Dorgu who met the delivery from close range to salvage a point. But the big question is: did he also salvage Carrick?

Michael Carrick has insisted he remains the right man to lead Manchester United and will not walk away despite the club being marooned in the relegation zone.

United came from 2-0 and 4-2 down to claim a last-gasp 4-4 draw against Aston Villa on another wild day at Old Trafford.It means United still only have one Premier League win to their name this season and are languishing in 18th position, a point adrift of safety, heading into the international break when the Old Trafford hierarchy must decide whether to keep faith with Carrick or appoint their third manager this year.

Carrick cut a spiky figure when asked about his future by Sky Sports and whether he would walk away.

“That’s not going to happen,” Carrick said, before asking “will there?” when it was put to him that there would “clearly” be conversations about his future.

“We haven’t won enough games, but I expect to move forward and keep working on the things we’ve been working on and showing a lot of good in the game today,” he said. “Tighten up on some things and start winning football matches.”

"That's not going to happen" 🗣️ Michael Carrick responds to the notion that he could resign as Manchester United head coach 🔴 https://t.co/q1fBKSXL7l

Asked later if he had seen enough to turn the situation around, the United head coach added: “Yeah, 100 per cent. I think there’s more than enough. Goals change games and you’ve got to deal with it, and it’s part of something we have to improve on drastically, but there’s more than enough.”Carrick scoffed at talk of United being in a relegation battle. “We’re in November,” he said. “I don’t like this situation where we are and where we’re at. But we can do something about it.”

Roy Keane, the former United captain, likened Carrick to a “politician”. “It’s hard to believe what’s coming out of the United camp because we can’t even be sure they’re being honest with themselves. It’s just words,” he said. “It’s obviously difficult for the manager. Under pressure, no doubt. He talks a lot but doesn’t say much. I don’t know if that’s a tactic. Like a politician.

“He keeps saying we need to tighten up and there’s things we need to work on. But they better get moving on that.”

Diogo Dalot’s second-half substitution was cheered by the home supporters and the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe again came under fierce attack from fans, who held up a banner in the Stretford End that read: “We don’t want a new stadium. We want new owners.” It is understood the banner was later confiscated by stewards.

Carrick defended Dalot’s contributions after another dismal showing from the Portugal defender and claimed the fans were “right behind” the players, despite growing discontent in the stands.

“I understand the frustration, I understand the disappointment of the supporters, so I get it. We’re all frustrated, we’re all disappointed,” Carrick said.

“Diogo, he gives absolutely everything. He’s played in different positions, he’s played left-back, he’s played really well at times. He gives a penalty away today, he knows that. Maybe he can do a little bit better, he’s made a mistake, but he cares an awful lot and he’s giving everything.

“I like what he brings to the team, I like what he brings to the group, I like what he brings to the whole environment and the culture that we’ve got.”

Asked if Dalot needed taking out of the team for his own good, Carrick: “Picking a team and who plays the next game, that’s a whole different decision, but it’s a whole different game that we’ve got to look forward to now.

“They [the fans] are desperate to get behind us and for us to give them something to go on and shout about. There’s frustration and disappointment at times, we all feel that. But they are right behind the boys and were at the final whistle as well.”

Unai Emery stormed straight down the tunnel before the final whistle, furious at his team’s failure to see out the game.

“We are disappointed, frustrated because in minute 90 we are winning 2-4,” the Villa manager said. “We will accept the result because we have won three and drawn three in last matches and we’re doing well. But today we have lost two points.”

With four Premier League games in progress the picture is ever-changing, but United are currently 19th in the Premier League table. The club, famously, were relegated in 1974 with the coup de grâce applied by Denis Law’s backheel when the Scot was playing in a City shirt. In this piece, James Ducker looks back on the previous occasions when one of the world’s biggest clubs has flirted with calamity.

When Villa dropped into the Championship, it did not change the fact they were the biggest club in the Midlands. No matter what Tom Brady does at Birmingham City, that’s not changing any time soon. They sought and achieved promotion by raiding Brentford.

Nobody was complaining about a sleeping giant taking Dean Smith, Ezri Konsa or Ollie Watkins and potentially stalling Brentford’s progression.

Nor was it suggested hiring Emery from Villarreal was an odd move given that the Spanish side had recently won the Europa League and reached the latter stages of the Champions League.

Michael Carrick says he has been given no assurances about his future beyond this afternoon’s crucial game against Aston Villa at Old Trafford.United are searching for only their second Premier League win of the season and first in 70 days after the club’s worst start to a campaign for 40 years piled the pressure on Carrick.They dropped into the relegation zone last night following Nottingham Forest’s victory over Manchester City and will be bottom by the end of the weekend if they lose to Villa and Crystal Palace and Sunderland both win.The Old Trafford hierarchy opted to give Carrick more time to try to turn their season around following a 3-0 hammering by Bournemouth and 4-1 drubbing in Como, since when United have been beaten 2-0 by Chelsea and recovered from two goals down to overcome Roma 3-2 in the Champions League on Tuesday night.Asked if he had been told outright he would still be in charge next week, Carrick said: “No - no. Just carry on as absolute normal.”Pressed on when he felt his future was uncertain, the head coach added: “No, no. Whatever happens and what’s going to happen is going to happen in terms of the game, we’ve got to prepare right.“I’m really looking forward to playing at home on the back of the other night. The supporters are hopefully looking forward to coming and energised and feeling good about what they might see and we’ve got to repay that.”Another defeat would leave the United board with a big decision to make around Carrick’s future at a time when they are under severe attack from the fanbase.United’s game against Roma was briefly interrupted when tennis balls were thrown on to the pitch in the first half of a game notable for more furious protests against the Glazers and Sir Jim Ratcliffe.Three people were arrested by Greater Manchester Police for throwing items on to the pitch and are understood to have been hit with automatic three-year football banning orders as a consequence. More in-stadium demonstrations are expected today with regular match going fans encouraged not to buy alcohol or drinks inside Old Trafford and again release green and gold balloons before kick-off.Green and gold were the club’s original colours as Newton Heath and have become a symbol of protest against the ownership. Asked why there had been such a big drop-off from last season, Carrick added: “It’s just inconsistency, that’s within games,” he said.“It can be a number of things, it’s never just one thing: a bit of decision-making, a bit of concentration, things going against us in certain points, sometimes we haven’t helped ourselves. So there’s no excuses for it, it is what it is. The great thing is we can do something about it.”

#1041. Peter Storey: Arsenal double winner dies aged 81

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Arsenal confirmed Storey’s death in a club statement on Tuesday

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Arsenal have announced the death of their former midfielder Peter Storey at the age of 81.

Having joined the Gunners as an apprentice in 1961, Storey made his first-team debut for the club in October 1965, and went on to stay at the club for a further 12 years.

A club statement on Tuesday read: "Everyone at Arsenal is deeply saddened by the passing of 1970-71 Double Winner, Peter Storey.

"All our thoughts are with his family and loved ones at this incredibly sad time. Rest in peace, Peter."

Arsenal also confirmed that the club will pay tribute to Storey during their Champions League fixture against Borussia Dortmund, which takes place on 24 November.

Storey initially started his Arsenal career at full-back before moving into midfield and winning the Fairs Cup in 1970.

During the 1970-71 campaign, Storey featured prominently in the Arsenal team that completed the double, playing an important role in their FA Cup triumph.

He scored a stoppage-time penalty against Stoke in the semi-finals to force a replay, before the Gunners went on to lift the trophy.

With 501 total appearances for Arsenal, Storey ranks as their eighth highest appearance maker of all time. Departing north London in 1977, he joined Fulham prior to retiring in 1978.

At international level, Storey received an England call-up in 1971 and was capped on 19 occasions.

Arsenal are due to play their first game after Storey’s death on Saturday when they face Newcastle at St James’ Park.

The Gunners headed into the international break with a five-point cushion at the top of the table after winning nine of their opening 10 Premier League matches.

Their nearest challengers are currently Brighton, who are also the only team to beat them this season.

Manchester City are a further point adrift after losing three matches in a row prior to the international break.

SpaceX has a message for itself, and for the spacecraft set to make history today (Nov. 13): Don't panic.

The company's Starship megarocket will conduct its 15th test flight this afternoon, a landmark liftoff that will feature the first-ever attempt to catch both of its stages with its launch tower's "chopstick" arms.

On Thursday (Nov. 12), SpaceX rolled the Flight 15 upper stage, a vehicle known as Ship 42, out to the launch pad at its Starbase site in South Texas to prep. The company shared photos of the move on X, and in two of those shots we can see some intriguing words inked on the spacecraft: "Don't panic."

The phrase is familiar to fans of Douglas Adams' sci-fi classic "The Hitchhiker's Guide to the Galaxy": In the novel, the electronic guidebook that helps travelers find their way across the cosmos has "Don't panic!" on its cover.

And Ship 42 itself is connected to the beloved book, by virtue of its serial number. In "The Hitchhiker's Guide," a supercomputer named Deep Mind is asked to come up with "the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe, and everything." It thinks for 7.5 million years and comes up with "42."

SpaceX founder and CEO Elon Musk has voiced his affection for "The Hitchhiker's Guide" in the past — and he has already paid tribute to it with a well-placed "Don't panic."

The debut launch of SpaceX's Falcon Heavy rocket back in February 2018 sent Musk's red Tesla Roadster into orbit around the sun, with a spacesuit-clad mannequin named Starman at the wheel and its entertainment display programmed to read "Don't panic!"

Starship Flight 15 is scheduled to launch today during a 75-minute window that opens at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT; 4:45 p.m. local Texas time). You can watch it here at Space.com.

If all goes according to plan, Starship's Super Heavy first stage will come back to Starbase for a chopsticks catch about 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

Ship 42, meanwhile, will head to orbit, a destination that Starship reached for the first time on Flight 14, which took place on Sept. 28. Ship 42 will deploy 26 of SpaceX's next-gen Starlink V3 satellites today — the second batch of the spacecraft to reach orbit. (The first set of 26 were delivered on Flight 14).

Ship 42 will stay up for a while after that, circling Earth 14 times before coming back for its own chopsticks catch on Saturday afternoon (Nov. 14), 22.5 hours after launch.

That's the plan, anyway; SpaceX will only go through with a Ship catch attempt if all systems on the vehicle look good. If there are any problems, the company will divert to a splashdown in the Pacific Ocean, near either Hawaii or Chile.

Both of Starship's stages — Super Heavy and the Ship — are designed to be rapidly reusable. And "rapidly" is a bit of understatement: SpaceX wants to launch 10,000 Starship missions per year by 2030, Musk has said.

The chopsticks-catch strategy is a big part of that vision. Bringing both Starship stages directly back to the launch mount will greatly reduce the time needed for inspection, refurbishment and reflight, according to SpaceX.

The company has already caught Super Heavy on three previous Starship test flights. It has never tried to do so with Ship, instead targeting ocean splashdowns with the upper stage.

The double catch attempt may be unprecedented, but SpaceX seems to be taking its own advice: There's no panic around Flight 15 or its bold goals.

"I'd say it's more likely than not that this succeeds next flight," Musk said last month, during SpaceX's third-quarter earnings call.

Michael Wall is the Spaceflight and Tech Editor for Space.com and joined the team in 2010. He has a Ph.D. in evolutionary biology from the University of Sydney, Australia, a bachelor's degree from the University of Arizona, and a graduate certificate in science writing from the University of California, Santa Cruz. #1039. Hiding remotes and unplugging TVs: How Celebrity Race Across the World cut Jeff Stelling off from football

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Exclusive interview: Former Soccer Saturday host Stelling is a contestant in the latest series of the hit adventure travel show which will see him traverse South East Asia

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Jeff Stelling has revealed that producers would unplug televisions and hide remotes during filming of Celebrity Race Across the World, which left the veteran sports broadcaster completely cut off from football and his beloved Hartlepool United.

Stelling is taking part in the latest series of the hit adventure travel show, teaming with his son Matt in a 4,660-mile race from the Malaysian city of Kuching to the finish line in Melbourne, Australia on a budget of £26 a day.

The former Soccer Saturday presenter, who ended over 30 years of service with Sky Sports in May 2023, is a passionate lifelong Hartlepool fan and serves as honorary president of the National League club.

But as he traversed the depths of South East Asia with no phone and limited technology, he was left completely in the dark about the club’s performance at the tail-end of the 2025/26 season.

“We couldn’t get any football scores at all because we’ve got no way [of finding them out],” Stelling told The Independent.

“If you’re within your checkpoints, if there’s a TV in your room, they [the producers] make sure it’s either disconnected or else they don’t give you a remote, so they make sure that that’s taken away. You’ve got no contact.”

The fourth series of the show, which aired its first episode on Wednesday, was filmed from February to April earlier this year.

During that time, Hartlepool experienced a mixed bag of results - going on their joint-best win streak of the season with three consecutive victories, only for that run to be ended by their heaviest defeat of the season: a 7-0 hammering at Wealdstone at the end of March.

Stelling says he was out of the loop for all of this, however, which allowed him to let his dreams run wild as the National League season approached its climax.

“For me, it meant I could fantasise that we were winning every game,” he added. “And then when we finished, I found out the truth that we hadn’t been winning every game.”

Stelling was speaking on behalf of Enterprise as he fronts the ‘Local Legends’ campaign, which strives to celebrate the unsung heroes that give their time for non-league clubs week in, week out.

Hartlepool, who have spent six of the last eight seasons in non-league, ended last season in ninth, 12 points adrift of the National League play-off places.

His agony without any knowledge of the Pools’ performance was not a shared experience with his youngest son, though, with Matt a Brighton supporter.

“Well obviously, my relationship with this son’s a bit stressed because he’s a Brighton fan!” Stelling joked, whose older son meanwhile follows his father’s lead in supporting Hartlepool.

“No, we’ve always gotten on really well,” he continued, “but it’s sort of challenging for both of us, but probably more for him, that you are going to spend six weeks, 24 hours a day, with your dad - often sharing a bed or sharing the same floor.

“Different generations have got different views of things, so inevitably, over that period of time, in the sort of intense situation that you’re in, there are inevitably going to be occasions when you’ve got to bite your tongue, on both sides.

“But it was brilliant. As I say, we were close before. We’re probably even closer afterwards.”

#1038. US Supreme Court rebuffs White House effort to cut research grants

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Max Kozlov is a senior reporter with Nature in Washington DC.

Dan Garisto is a freelance reporter in Syracuse, New York.

The Supreme Court’s decision not to take up a dispute over federal research grants hands a win to scientists.Credit: Kevin Dietsch/Getty

The US Supreme Court has dealt a blow to the Trump administration’s efforts to terminate research grants it deemed at odds with its political priorities.

The court said today that it would, for now, not intervene in a landmark legal battle over the cancellation of research grants by the US National Science Foundation (NSF) and four other federal agencies. The court’s decision leaves in place several lower-court rulings that came out this year and last and required the reinstatement of hundreds of cancelled awards while a lawsuit brought by a group of scientists against the government proceeds.

Since early 2025, US President Donald Trump’s administration has cancelled thousands of grants from agencies such as the US National Institutes of Health (NIH) and the NSF. Many of the cancelled grants were for studies that contained terms that the administration said ran counter to its priorities, such as “climate change,” “equity” and “gender”. In response, a group of University of California researchers whose grants had been terminated sued the administration. Lower courts have repeatedly sided with the scientists, finding that the government had penalized academic researchers based on their viewpoints and that this likely violated the US Constitution’s First Amendment, which protects freedom of speech and other activities.

Judge rules against NIH grant cuts — and calls them discriminatory

Judge rules against NIH grant cuts — and calls them discriminatory

The Supreme Court’s refusal to hear the case is a relief to scientists whose work was left in limbo, and leaves protections for their reinstated funding in place. “The denial is terrific news,” says Claudia Polsky, a lawyer for the University of California researchers. The denial came only three days after the case was considered on 13 November, and none of the nine justices publicly dissented from the decision. “Those are all of the best signs one could have that the Supreme Court really did not buy the government's argument,” Polsky says.

The White House referred Nature to the US Department of Justice, which said that it would “continue to litigate” the order by one of the lower courts that “currently prevents the cancellation of certain federal research grants supporting diversity, equity, and inclusion initiatives within the University of California system”.

The Supreme Court’s decision not to take up the case now is not the final word on grant terminations. The lower courts found that the researchers were likely to succeed, rather than issuing a final judgment. Once a final ruling is issued, it could be appealed, potentially bringing the case back before the Supreme Court.

The case kicked off in June 2025, when Neeta Thakur, a physician who studies marginalized communities, and five other researchers at the University of California who had had federal grants terminated sued the Trump administration. The researchers argued that the cancellations were arbitrary and unlawfully penalized scientists whose work clashed with the White House’s political agenda.

The same month, judge Rita Lin at the US District Court for the Northern District of California ordered the NSF, the Environmental Protection Agency and the National Endowment for the Humanities to reinstate the University of California researchers’ grants. The plaintiffs had a “substantial likelihood that their funding was terminated based on the viewpoint expressed in their grant proposals”, Lin wrote.

Can NIH-funded research on racism and health survive Trump’s cuts?

Can NIH-funded research on racism and health survive Trump’s cuts?

In August 2025, the Supreme Court issued a ruling in a separate case about the termination of around 800 NIH grants. The court ruled that federal district courts — such as the one that originally ruled in favour of Thakur — cannot reinstate cancelled grants by invoking a law called the Administrative Procedure Act (APA), which requires federal agencies to follow proper procedures and justify their decisions. Some lower courts had used this reasoning to reinstate terminated grants.

It's unclear what caused the anomaly, which occurred 10 minutes into flight.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

United Launch Alliance's Vulcan Centaur rocket suffered an anomaly during its launch today (Nov. 15), resulting in the loss of 40 Amazon internet satellites.

The Vulcan Centaur lifted off from Florida's Cape Canaveral Space Force Station today at 12:40 p.m. ET (1740 GMT), hauling 40 satellites for the Amazon Leo broadband constellation toward low Earth orbit (LEO). But they never got there.

"Based on data received by our Launch Director, we confirm that the Vulcan vehicle launched from Space Launch Complex 41 suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight and failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit," ULA said in an update on X today, 50 minutes after launch. "Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today."

Today's launch was supposed to be a bounce-back mission for the Vulcan Centaur, the successor to ULA's workhorse Atlas V rocket.

Vulcan debuted in January 2024 and had four total flights under its belt before today. On two of those missions — its second, in October 2024, and its fourth, in February of this year — the rocket experienced an issue with one of its solid rocket boosters (SRBs).

In both cases, an SRB nozzle burned through and fell off about 30 seconds after launch. Vulcan Centaur overcame the problem on both launches, successfully delivering its payloads to their designated orbits. But the U.S. Space Force was concerned enough that it decided to pause national security launches on Vulcan until ULA addressed the problem. (Vulcan's third and fourth launches were Space Force missions.)

ULA worked hard on that front and got Vulcan ready to return to flight, which finally occurred today after nine months..

"The integrated team has made great strides in improving our understanding of the SRB anomaly that occurred on the previous Vulcan flight and have identified several potential contributors, which have been mitigated through design and process improvements to the nozzle," the company said in an Oct. 28 update.

That nozzle work apparently paid off: The SRBs appeared to perform as expected during today's launch. But a different, more serious problem cropped up today, and Vulcan Centaur could not overcome it.

Today's launch was supposed to help build out Amazon's broadband constellation in LEO, which was previously called Project Kuiper but is now known as Amazon Leo. It will eventually compete with SpaceX's Starlink network, which has been up and running for several years.

Amazon Leo will consist of more than 3,200 satellites. Before today, about 400 of them had reached space on 15 launches, which were conducted by three different rockets — the Atlas V, SpaceX's Falcon 9 and Arianespace's Ariane 6. Today's launch was the first such mission for the Vulcan Centaur, which explains ULA's name for the launch — Vulcan Leo 1.

The Amazon Leo launch was part of a very busy stretch in spaceflight. SpaceX launched its Starship megarocket on Friday (Nov. 13), on a test mission that featured the first-ever catch of the vehicle's Ship upper stage. And Rocket Lab launched its 100th-ever mission early Saturday morning (Nov. 14), sending a private Japanese Earth-observing satellite to orbit.

Editor's note: This story was updated at 12:50 p.m. ET on Nov. 15 with news of liftoff, then again at 1:45 p.m. ET with news of the anomaly and loss of the mission.

#1036. Jeff Stelling: We’d have two or three beers the night before Soccer Saturday – it was brilliant

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Stelling speaks to Will Castle about his Sky Sports exit, his relationship with old Soccer Saturday colleagues and the new age of punditry, spearheaded by Jason Cundy and Jamie O’Hara

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

There is a changing of the guard in football punditry and the 17th floor of talkSPORT Towers provides a snapshot of its evolution. Listeners, pick your poison.

In the morning, you can tune into the veteran of sports broadcasting. Jeff Stelling, once the voice of our Saturday afternoons, hosts your breakfast show alongside Ally McCoist from Mondays through to Wednesdays. It’s classic stuff. While most of his Soccer Saturday colleagues have since been consigned to the scrapheap, Stelling still very much has his foothold in the industry and as such brings us a taste of the ‘good old days’.

However, his old-school bread-and-butter style admittedly feels like it’s on its way out, for better or worse. Because in the dark of the night, during the prime-time slot, things go a bit blinky-eyed manic. The seat occupied by Stelling earlier that day is now filled by a man in a mask, shouting into a microphone. Jason Cundy and Jamie O’Hara are changing the pundit’s playbook with The Sports Bar; it’s chaotic, it’s crude and it does millions.

Never one to be behind the times, Stelling recognises the market for football media based largely on mockery nowadays. But don’t expect him to follow suit.

“I think there’s a place for it... not on one of my shows!” Stelling tells The Independent, who will not be showing up to work with a Derek McInnes mask any time soon.

“But Cundy and O’Hara, I think at that time of night... it’s irreverent to say the least. Obviously they take the mickey out of each other mercifully, Cundy with his Ange mask and so on. And they take the mickey out of callers as well. I think it works perfectly well at that stage. But you can’t have that all the way through.”

Pundits increasingly find themselves leaning into their club loyalties for the sake of entertainment, when purists would argue that the position should be neutral. Stelling, admittedly, was never completely down the middle; he was and still is known for his die-hard fandom of Hartlepool United, where he serves as honorary president. It’s fuelled his love of non-league, which is why he found himself at Woking FC on this grey October afternoon, fronting Enterprise’s Local Legends campaign which strives to celebrate the volunteers that keep clubs like his alive.

He wants to incentivise more people to get involved with their community club, hailing the mental health benefits for fans. “ Whether they've got problems at home, whether they've got financial difficulties, whether they've got health worries, it's almost therapy,” Stelling said. “So the football club, massively important to the community.”

But in the context of ‘Cundyism’, Stelling feels his Hartlepool ties benefited him in during his three-decade stint in front of the cameras.

“It’s one of the things that has helped me in my career, being a Hartlepool fan, because if I were a Liverpool or Man United or Tottenham fan, I’d have found things much more difficult,” he adds. “People would never have accepted that I was neutral, which I’ve always tried to be. People say, ‘Who’s your Premier League team?’ I say, ‘I haven’t got one,’ and I genuinely have not got one.

“But the growth of that [less neutrality in punditry], everybody seems quite happy now. They shout from the rooftop who their team is. Football is incredibly tribal, and I think that’s sometimes one of the problems.”

Stelling brought his legendary stint with Sky Sports to an end over three years ago, presenting his last Soccer Saturday in May 2023 after 29 years behind the desk. He was the last of a banished era, with the show’s once-regulars - Charlie Nicholas, Phil Thompson and Matt Le Tissier - all axed by the broadcaster following sweeping personnel changes in 2020. Chris Kamara, of “Unbelievable Jeff!” fame, followed out the exit door two years later amid his deteriorating health, diagnosed with speech apraxia - though he has since made a remarkable recovery after undergoing experimental treatment in Mexico.

Stelling, however, called time on his own accord after simply falling out of love with the job. “It was fully on my own terms,” he says. “ I had been intended to leave when Phil Thompson, Charlie Nicholas and Matt Le Tissier were sacked, but I was asked to stay on for another year to help bed in the new boys, then  I actually stayed longer than that for all sorts of different reasons. But I felt the time had come.

“I was finding that it had become, to a degree, a chore. I used to love going out there, loved working on Soccer Saturday, used to love building up to it, doing statistics and stories at home. And being there on the Saturday, the best day of the week, every week.

“I'd lost that feeling. And because I'd lost that feeling, I'd done it for 30 years, I thought it was time maybe to see what life outside Sky was like.”

Stelling was anxious about his own health during his final days at Sky, but got out before the “mental toll” became too much. “It was a mental stress and I feared if I carried on, it would make me unwell,” he admits. “But I was never physically unwell. I just got to the stage where honestly, I didn’t want to go in and do it.”

Even the idea of the show doesn’t make him long for the days of old. “I don’t miss it,” Stelling asserts. But he can still cherish the memories with the old Soccer Saturday crew, especially those outside of the studio.

“We used to get together on a Friday night and I’m not ashamed to say we’d have two or three beers, and it was brilliant,” he says. “They were just great, great nights.”

Holding celebrity value in their own right, the odd notable name from the world of football would join the party. “I know [we went out with] David Moyes once, Delia Smith, Chris Wilder - happy to spend time with them,” he recalls. “But it was the company of the boys, really.”

A group that made the 3pm blackout not just tolerable but enjoyable, hearts broke when the clock ran out on Stelling’s cohort. Fans of that time may therefore find solace to know that, to buck a time-old trend of television, their friendship has survived beyond the screen.

“We live all over the country so it’s difficult to get together, but we do get together from time to time, and bump into each other at various events and things,” he says. “We’re all in touch. We were all best mates, really. We still are.”

Thomas Sorensen attributes 'a bit of a bust-up' with then-manager Martin O'Neill as the reason his spell at Aston Villa came to an end, 20 years ago.

The stopper was a reliable presence between the sticks for Aston Villa from 2003 to 2007, only to find himself out of favour throughout 2007/08.

Sorensen admits it was the most difficult time of his career, but he found a new lease of life after making the move to newly-promoted Stoke City the following season.

Sorensen told FourFourTwo: "We had a bit of a bust-up. I got injured in pre-season and they brought Scott Carson in from Liverpool.

"I was contacted by the Danish press and said I couldn’t quite understand that situation: ‘Why would he come in if he wasn’t going to play?’

"It wasn’t ill-intended by me, but I don’t know if that upset Martin. He’s definitely not on my Christmas card list.

"I was dropped into the youth team and prevented from moving to Tottenham. That was probably the toughest period of my career.

The best features, fun and footballing quizzes, straight to your inbox every week.

"I just worked my socks off for other opportunities and luckily that came at Stoke."

Sorensen admits that he had his doubts about that move, saying: "It was a bit of a gamble, but it reminded me of going back to my Sunderland days.

"Tony Pulis was very old school and they had that team spirit. I felt at home in that environment and I loved the challenge.

"It was an opportunity to show people that there was still life in the old dog. It obviously went a lot better than we thought. I signed for one year and seven years later I was still there.

"It was us against the world. Everyone hated us because of the way we played – the physicality and the long throws.

"Having that unity made it even better. We had some great seasons there. Pulis was really good at pitting us against everyone else, like Match of the Day, because we were last on and everyone was talking badly about the way we played.

"Everyone bought into that. Fighting for each other gave us that success. The atmosphere at the Britannia was incredible."

He has been a Newcastle United season ticket holder since 2000 and has a deep knowledge on the history and culture of football shirts.

#1034. Kane bends game to his will on record-breaking night

One day it will have to end for Harry Kane, but for now, almost 12 years into his England life, there is still no matching the wisdom and influence he has accumulated over all those games and all those goals for his country.

This would have been a great night by any measure for a man collecting his record-breaking 126th England cap. There was a handshake from Peter Shilton, now deposed as king of caps, and a flourish by Kane of his recently acquired Ballon d’Or, once his four children had accompanied him on to the pitch. These are the nights of which dreams are made, and yet – given the defining feature of Kane’s career – there was one more thing to accomplish.

That was a goal from the man who has ploughed relentlessly past the two great England individual landmarks of caps and goals. His second-half penalty won the game and, although he is not infallible from the spot, he is as close to that status as England have ever had. Age has not yet run him down, he can still bend the game to his will, and when it comes to the pressure moments, his longevity seems to offer the upper hand.

This was always going to be Kane’s night, with a great banner on the west side of the stadium paying tribute to the England captain. The Prince of Wales was in attendance for the occasion, too. Luka Modric presented his former Tottenham Hotspur team-mate with a keepsake from the Croatian football federation. Kane had to wait for the second half for the most valuable offering of all.

After the hour, the Danish referee Morten Krogh was advised by his VAR Bastian Dankert to take a second look at a corner tangle involving Jarell Quansah, and decided to award the second-half penalty from which Kane scored. It was certainly clumsy, but these grapples have been overlooked by referees in the past. The 27th successfully converted penalty of the Kane England era followed, and the man himself played the full game.

Afterwards, Kane made a point of thanking the Football Association for organising it all, although it was also clear that this was no less than he expected. “It’s important to recognise the great players,” he said, “and it’s not something we have always done over the years.”

"It's a perfect opportunity now on Sunday to try and prove ourselves" 👊🏻 🏴󠁧󠁢󠁥󠁮󠁧󠁿 Harry Kane looks ahead to England's matchup against World Cup winners Spain, following tonight's 2-1 win against Croatia. https://t.co/m2OCkuN5kY

If the sentiment was a little awkwardly articulated, he is certainly right on the key point: so many England careers have ended abruptly at tournament elimination or elsewhere. Yet here was one being celebrated with the man himself, in what might even be argued to be his prime. Kane, 33, was asked again as to how long he might continue and did not rule out going on to 40, “if I’m performing at the highest level”.

That was a nod to Modric, a second-half substitute at the age of 41 and now on 207 caps for Croatia and almost 1,200 senior games. This Croatia team still seem unable to part company with their greatest player, despite his struggles against England in the seven-goal defeat in Rijeka. On this occasion, Croatia were much better.

It should have been more straightforward for England. They had taken the lead through Morgan Rogers midway through the first half and had dominated the first hour. But Quansah’s mistake gave Croatia an equaliser, and after Kane’s penalty England were fortunate to survive on occasions.

"It's a calamity of errors for England defensively!" 🇭🇷 Sučić equalises for Croatia https://t.co/GBxTSptUuF

“It was a tight match – a tough one,” Thomas Tuchel, the England manager, said. “We didn’t take our chances when we had chances, so it stayed a tight match. It cannot be glamorous and super-exciting [all the time]. It has to be serious and determined. We wanted a final on Sunday in Spain and we have that.”

The win means that England’s game in Madrid on Sunday against Spain, who beat the Czech Republic and lead the Nations League group by three points, has some bite to it. Another England win would mean they would overtake Spain on goal difference and win the group ahead of the Nations League quarter-finals in March.

This was one game when the players might have wondered if they were due more from a Wembley crowd that went through the motions in the first half and scarcely returned for the second. For the first hour, England dominated a Croatia side who often invited six blue shirts into their back line. Tuchel said his decision to select Dan Burn in the left-sided centre-half position over the left-footed Jarrad Branthwaite was almost split – a “51 per cent decision”.

England would break through just once, when Rogers got enough of his laces on an awkward Jude Bellingham cross deflected behind him and the shot brushed Josko Gvardiol on the way in.

Trent Alexander-Arnold started his third England game of the autumn and the right-back spent most of it in midfield. From the left it was his pass to Bellingham on the right wing that prefaced the cross for the Rogers goal.

The catastrophe of the defeat last month for Croatia meant they were naturally conservative. Nevertheless, in Martin Baturina, the 23-year-old Como attacking midfielder, they have another fine talent. When Modric did come on, he was applauded on all sides of Wembley. The home fans would later boo the arrival of Ben White, still not forgiven for his 2022 mid-tournament World Cup departure.

The equaliser was a Quansah error when the defender tried to head a loose corner back to Jordan Pickford and did not make the distance. Petar Sucic intervened and pushed it home with a right foot. Three minutes later it was judged a foul on Quansah by Ivan Smolcic when he pulled the Englishman down and the referee Krogh eventually gave the penalty.

Kane scored that and the substitute James Garner had a goal disallowed in the closing stages of the game, which were much less comfortable for England.

England manager Thomas Tuchel, speaking to ITV: “Good win. We wanted this win desperately and I think we deserved it. I think it was hard work against a good opponent. It took us a while to grow into the game but after 15 minutes I think we did OK, got the goal and got better and more confident and had some good actions and good chances, good half-chances.

“Got a little bit sloppy at the very end of the first half, started the second half very good, didn’t score the second goal, conceded from a set piece, and then showed a good reaction.

“We got the job done and it was important because it was a special occasion for Harry [Kane] and he scored the winner, so perfect evening.”

On whether England were sloppy when they conceded: “It was maybe only three or four minutes before we gave passes away and especially in a moment when we were clearly the better team, we came with a very strong reaction after the half-time, had a beautiful chance created from Declan Rice and they blocked it on the line. It was like our third goal was coming and we had some easy ball losses in our own half that killed our momentum.

“An awkward moment in our box can always happen. It’s important to react and we did it.”

On his defenders: “Good. It was demanding for Dan Burn and also for Jarell [Quansah] because they [Croatia] play with a back five and have two number 10s in between the lines.

“It was a lot of work to do, a lot of communication but they did very well.”

On what will be better against Spain on Sunday: “I don’t know. Everything will be different. Completely different scenario, completely different setup, but I’m very positive that we will get what we want.”

England put in an the-Lord-Mayor’s-show performance following their 7-0 victory over Croatia. But it was still good enough to beat the same opponents 2-1 on the night Harry Kane celebrated his 126th record-breaking cap at Wembley.

Kane capped the night with the winning goal from the penalty spot, but a poor second-half showing – after Morgan Rogers had opened the scoring in the 24th minute – allowed Petar Sucic to equalise, aided by a dreadful mistake by Jarell Quansah.

England captain Harry Kane, speaking to ITV: “An incredible gesture, reception at the start of the game. Once the game starts, it’s about getting the win, getting the three points. We’re playing against a tough team, a team that wanted to prove something tonight.

“I think for large spells of the game we done well. Got a little bit tired towards the end but overall a really great win and sets up a great game on Sunday now.”

On how he was feeling as he stepped up for his penalty: “Same as ever. I missed my last one for Bayern, so I think it’s always important to try and bounce back with the next one. Try to not miss two in a row but executing. I practised yesterday like I always do and it’s just about going out there and doing it out on the pitch.

“I think we gave away a few too many easy balls, especially in our own half, which killed the momentum a little bit. I think we had enough chances to score two or three but we’re playing against a good team.

“We’re in the midst of a run of tough games for club and country, so you can’t always expect things to be perfect. Of course, we know we can improve on a few bits and we will need to if we want to win on Sunday, but ultimately it’s about getting a win tonight.”

On aiming to beat Spain and top the group: “100%. After the first game when we lost here against them, we knew we left a bit out there. We knew we could’ve done a bit better. We said to ourselves let’s win every game until the next one and see what happens. It’s the perfect opportunity now on Sunday to try and prove ourselves.”

Thomas Tuchel tells ITV: “A good win, we wanted this desperately, we deserved it. It was hard work against a good opponent.” We will bring you more from the England head coach shortly.

Harry Kane has told ITV that it was an “incredible reception” for him at the start of a “really good win”. We will bring you the captain’s full quotes shortly.

While top spot in the group is still up for grabs, England have booked their place in the Nations League quarter-finals, which will take place in March 2027.

The winners of those ties progress to the Nations League Finals in June.

Harry Kane has now scored 92 goals in 126 appearances for England.

Few expect Jobe to be better than his older brother. While Jobe will make his England debut just two months after turning 21, Jude’s first cap came aged 17. Younger siblings have significantly more chance of becoming elite athletes. If two siblings both become professional, the little sibling is significantly more likely to enjoy the better career.

Jude and Jobe Bellingham could become the first brothers to start for England since Gary and Phil Neville took to the field together 19 years ago, with Jobe included in his first senior squad.

Jack and Bobby Charlton are the only other brothers to play together for England in the post-war period.

“It’s quite special, to be honest. It’s such a huge bonus on top of something that’s already so special and so great. To be called up for England is a dream itself and I’ve been so proud to have the opportunity to represent England at every age group.

“I don’t have the words, really. I think it’s only emotion that could describe it, and, hopefully, if that time does come, you’ll see a lot of emotion from people, and definitely from my family.”

“I think I maybe underappreciated how big it was going to be, how big the reaction was going to be,” he told the BBC.

“I think the actual moment when Ronaldo said my name, it’s strange, it’s almost like a movie.

“In the moment, it was like in slow motion and the confetti was supposed to fall and all this, but when I watched it back, I had my hand to my mouth and maybe a couple of seconds and I was out, but in the actual moment, it felt like I was doing it for a minute.

“It was a really unique feeling because it is different to playing a game or scoring a goal, because it is so individual, it is nothing you can kind of do.

“Your mind is playing games with you the whole night, whether it is going to be you or not.

“So, when he actually said my name, it was just a crazy emotion.”

To the exclusive club of Billy Wright, Sir Bobby Charlton, Bobby Moore and Peter Shilton, the name Harry Kane will be added on Thursday night. It is only the fifth time that a new men’s England international appearance record has been set in the post-war era, with Kane preparing for his 126th England match to surpass a landmark that has stood for 36 years.

“I’ll be the first to congratulate him because I think he’s done it the right way,” says Shilton, who will be back at Wembley to metaphorically pass on the baton.

“He’s not coming on as a substitute; he’s been out there every game, doing his job. Records are there to be beaten and I couldn’t think of anybody better than Harry, not just on the pitch but off the pitch. I am very proud of the record and handing it to Harry makes it not quite as bad.

“I think striker is the hardest position to play and goalkeeper is the second hardest because of the responsibility you’ve got. But scoring goals is the most difficult thing and Harry’s record in the modern game is there to be seen.”

Thomas Tuchel has said Harry Kane was the deserved winner of the Ballon d’Or, with the England head coach describing the striker as “an extraordinary player”.

“He wins the Ballon d’Or, and deservedly so, and in the next game for England he gets the all-time record with 126 matches,” Tuchel said when announcing the latest squad.

“Thursday is a deserved occasion to celebrate an extraordinary player.”

Kane said: “It’s not about me – it’s about the team. I love coming to every England camp. I love playing every game and representing the country in the best way possible.”

Harry Kane starts for England in what will be a record 126th appearance for his country.

"This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Update for 6:25 p.m. ET: SpaceX has launched the Starship Flight 15 mission, but did skip the first stage Super Heavy booster landing. See launch video and our full Starship Flight 15 liftoff wrap.

Having reached orbit for the first time with Starship last time out, SpaceX is looking to take a huge stride toward full reusability with Flight 15 — the first attempt to catch the megarocket's Ship upper stage, as the company eyes hourly launches by 2030.

SpaceX is targeting today (Nov. 13) for Starship's 15th flight, which will lift off from the company's Starbas site in South Texas. If all goes well, the mission — which you can watch here at Space.com — will end on Saturday (Nov. 14) with the first attempt at what SpaceX itself calls the "Holy Grail of rocketry": Catching both Starship's Super Heavy booster and Ship upper stage chopstick-style back at the launch pad.

"If successful, this will mark the first full recovery of an orbital launch system and a breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket," SpaceX wrote in its Flight 15 mission description.

The 75-minute Flight 15 launch window opens today at 5:45 p.m. EST (2245 GMT), and a number of Starship firsts are planned for early in the flight. For example, while SpaceX has caught three Super Heavy boosters and reused two of them to date, the first attempt to catch a next-gen Super Heavy "V3" vehicle will come today, around 6.5 minutes after liftoff.

If the Ship upper stage gets the go-ahead for orbital insertion, it will deploy 26 Starlink V3 satellites — designed especially for use on Starship — into low Earth orbit (LEO), starting about 35 minutes after launch. Then, 21 hours later, if "internally developed, and FAA-approved, conditions" for a return to Starbase and catch are met — including on-orbit assessment of Ship's heat shield by three of the V3 satellites — SpaceX will attempt to recover the orbital upper stage.

This landmark try will follow the first-ever Ship reentry over inhabited areas, as the vehicle will maneuver its way over sparsely populated regions of northern Mexico and southern Texas. (On previous missions, Ship has splashed down in the open ocean.) It will head back to Starbase and make a bellyflop maneuver as it descends to the site's Pad 2 before flipping itself vertical, ready for embrace of the launch tower's waiting mechanical arms.

"SpaceX will attempt to catch both the Super Heavy booster and Starship on the upcoming flight. If both are successful, it will mark the first time that all parts of an orbital rocket return to Earth intact," Elon Musk said via X, the social media platform he owns, on Nov. 6. "This is the critical breakthrough needed to make life multiplanetary."

Half of the system is already proven. With catching and reflying boosters largely established, the next and unprecedented step is catching Ship. This is no easy task. The vehicle, returning from orbital speeds, must survive the heat of reentry, make its way precisely back to the pad put itself in position to be caught by the tower's "chopstick" arms. The full recovery of an orbital launch system would, in the words of SpaceX, be a "breakthrough moment in making Starship a reliable, rapidly reusable rocket" and would open the "door to airplane-like cadence."

A successful catch would allow SpaceX to then work on refurbishing Ship for reflight, the next challenge of full reusability. Musk said in August in a SpaceX earnings call that the company will aim to refly the Super Heavy and Ship early next year.

SpaceX has a lot of experience with rocket reuse, as its workhorse Falcon 9 rocket pioneered the practice. But the company is eyeing another level of reflight with Starship: It's targeting roughly 10,000 launches of the megarocket per year by 2030, which works out to more than one launch per hour.

"We're aiming to reach 30+ Starship launches/day in 2030, which is ~10k annualized," Musk posted on X in August.

The company has repeated that figure to regulators. In comments filed with the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration in late October, it said that "SpaceX anticipates conducting 10,000 launches per year itself." Meanwhile, the recently signed National Space Transportation Policy aims to boost the U.S.'s capabilities to support more than 1,000 rocket launches per year by 2030.

Musk added that SpaceX's planned Starbase Louisiana site alone could support that many Starship launches. For context: SpaceX launched 165 Falcon 9 missions in 2025, and that was about half of the global total for orbital flights.

Why is SpaceX targeting this incredible increase in launch cadence? It wants to build satellite megaconstellations that dwarf anything the world has ever seen.

The company's V3 Starlink satellites are too large to fly efficiently on the Falcon 9. Each one of the next-gen spacecraft adds 1 terabit of capacity to SpaceX's broadband network, and the 26 flying on Flight 15 are equivalent to around 10 Falcon 9 launches packed with Starlink V2 Mini satellites, according to SpaceX. And the company wants to put a staggering 100,000 V3 Starlink satellites into orbit. (There are currently about 11,000 current-gen Starlink satellites in orbit, and that's by far the largest satellite network assembled to date.)

SpaceX's Starmind project blows even this figure out of the water. SpaceX wants to launch up to 1 million satellites to serve as orbital AI data centers, and it appears to be making the moves terrestrially regarding the hardware. On Nov. 10, German firm Singulus Technologies announced a contract worth more than 60 million euros for a solar cell production line for Starmind satellites, which SpaceX builds in Bastrop, Texas. Musk said the order covers equipment for 100 gigawatts of solar cells per year. In terms of orbital hardware, the project is only feasible if SpaceX can reach its targeted "airplane-like cadence."

The gap between SpaceX's vision and the situation today is vast. Starship flew four times in 2024 and five times in 2025, and Flight 15 would be its fourth launch of 2026. Musk said on the earnings call that he expects Starship to fly weekly at some point in the first half of 2027, and twice weekly or more by the end of that year. Starbase in Texas is currently authorized for 25 launches per year, and the Louisiana site is not expected to host a launch before 2029.

Even a perfect outing for Flight 15 and two clean catches will leave lots of work to do. SpaceX will then need to demonstrate reflight with Ship, after assessing the impact on its heat shield system. Then comes orbital refueling, which is a necessary step for any Starship trip beyond LEO and a requirement for SpaceX's commitment to NASA's Artemis program of moon exploration. It's unclear how many tanker flights and refuelings will be needed to make a lunar mission possible, but, whatever the number, Starship will probably need to be rapidly reusable. Another step is carrying people. SpaceX has tested life support hardware on the ground in a crew cabin for the moon lander version of Starship that it is building for NASA, but no Starship has flown with such a system.

There are no guarantees for Flight 15. Ship will only be cleared for a return to Starbase and a catch attempt if it meets safety checks after reaching orbit, which itself is an achievement not to be taken for granted. Flight controllers may end up needing to bring Ship down in the Pacific Ocean or divert its reentry into the Gulf late into flight.

Musk told investors last month that success on this flight is "more likely than not." Whatever happens today and on Saturday, the measure of Starship's progress will soon shift from whether SpaceX can catch a Ship to how quickly it can launch one again.

#1032. FA chair to examine Gianni Infantino’s Fifa World Cup sell-off plan documents

Please refresh the page or navigate to another page on the site to be automatically logged inPlease refresh your browser to be logged in

Gianni Infantino was forced to abandon his controversial plan earlier this year

Want to bookmark your favourite articles and stories to read or reference later? Start your Independent Membership today.

Football Association chair Debbie Hewitt is set to inspect documentation in person regarding Fifa’s deeply contentious World Cup private investment proposal, it is understood.

The global governing body dispatched a letter on 2 November to members of the Fifa Council – where Hewitt serves as a Fifa vice-president – offering them the opportunity to examine the files at its headquarters in Zurich.

Hewitt is believed to have taken up the offer, though a firm date for the trip remains unconfirmed. Uefa president Aleksander Ceferin is likewise thought to have agreed to attend.

Relations between Uefa and Fifa president Gianni Infantino broke down over the project, which involved creating a new entity named Fifa Forward Enterprise (FFE) to manage commercial and operational activities for both the men’s and women’s World Cups alongside other Fifa tournaments.

Under the blueprint, a minority shareholding in FFE was to be acquired by private investors, led by Thrive Capital, an entity established by Joshua Kushner, whose brother is the son-in-law of United States President Donald Trump.

The initiative was ultimately scrapped following opposition from Uefa and a pair of other continental confederations.

Hewitt’s career experience in private equity provides her with direct insight into the standard documentation and financial details expected in proposals of this nature.

Fifa issued the invitation after European representatives on the Fifa Council sent a formal letter on 19 October requesting clarity on several matters, including the FFE arrangement and disciplinary proceedings involving Folarin Balogun.

Provisions regarding non-disclosure agreements and the specific terms governing document inspection in Zurich have yet to be finalised.

Earlier on Tuesday, the French Football Federation formally endorsed Philippe Diallo’s bid for the Fifa presidency.

On Monday, Uefa confirmed that the 63-year-old had secured the support of national association delegates across its executive committee and the Fifa Council to challenge Infantino.

Disquiet over the FFE proposals prompted European football’s governing body to promise in August that it would put forward a credible challenger to Infantino.

Diallo’s domestic federation has now unanimously backed his campaign, stating: "World football is going through a pivotal period in its history. The challenges affecting its governance demand clear thinking and responsibility.

"Restoring trust, preserving the universality of football, rebuilding Fifa’s credibility, and placing the development of football in all regions of the world at the heart of its actions are essential issues for the entire international football community.

"By accepting this invitation, Philippe Diallo is responding to a desire to open a new chapter for the governance of world football."

Figures within Uefa had previously hoped that former Arsenal manager Arsene Wenger, who currently serves as Fifa’s chief of global football development, might enter the race, though he is believed to have declined the prospect last week.
